items.title: A buffer works best when pH = pKa — even though that means it's only half-effective
items.claim: A buffer is maximally effective at resisting pH change when [HA] = [A-], which means pH = pKa by Henderson-Hasselbalch. Counter-intuitively, this is when only half the acid is dissociated — not when you've added the most base.
items.prompt: Why does maximum buffering happen at half-neutralisation?

options.text: Because half-neutralisation is the only stable condition
Adding acid converts A- to HA and vice versa; the ratio [HA]/[A-] changes most slowly when the two are equal — small additions barely shift the log of the ratio, so pH barely changes
Buffers cannot work outside pH = pKa
Acid and base cancel only at pKa

items.reveal:
Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]).

If [HA] = [A-] (i.e. pH = pKa), then log term = 0 and small changes in [A-] or [HA] barely shift pH. Capacity is maximised within ±1 pH unit of pKa.

Move far from pKa and a buffer collapses: at pH = pKa + 2, [A-]/[HA] = 100; adding more acid takes it from 100 to 50 — only a 0.3 pH change at first, but the conjugate base is rapidly used up.

This is why biological buffers are tuned to the physiological pH they need to defend: phosphate (pKa2 = 7.2) inside cells, carbonate-bicarbonate (open system at pH 7.4) in blood. Choosing pKa to match the target pH is buffer design 101.
items.why: Maximum effectiveness coincides with 'only half the acid is reacted' — a useful surprise that follows directly from the log.

items.title: Chromium and copper break the Aufbau rule
items.claim: By the Aufbau principle, chromium should be [Ar] 4s2 3d4 and copper [Ar] 4s2 3d9. In reality they are [Ar] 4s1 3d5 and [Ar] 4s1 3d10 — both 'borrow' an electron from 4s to make the 3d subshell half-filled or full.
items.prompt: Why do these specific configurations win?

options.text: Quantum mechanics is approximate for transition metals
Half-filled (d5) and fully filled (d10) subshells have extra exchange-energy stability from maximising parallel-spin pairs; the small 4s/3d gap is outweighed by this stability
Cr and Cu have extra protons
Their ground states have not been measured properly

items.reveal:
Electrons with parallel spins in different orbitals reduce mutual repulsion via the exchange interaction. A half-filled subshell maximises the number of such parallel pairs.

For chromium, [Ar] 4s1 3d5 has six parallel-spin electrons across 4s and 3d, giving 15 exchange interactions. [Ar] 4s2 3d4 would have fewer parallel pairs (the 4s electrons must be paired). The exchange energy gain is about 100 kJ/mol — comfortably larger than the 4s/3d orbital energy gap.

Niobium, molybdenum, ruthenium, rhodium, palladium, silver, platinum and gold all show similar 'anomalies' in their ground-state configurations for the same reason. These aren't rule-breakers — they obey the deeper physics behind the rule.
items.why: Filling rules are simplifications. Real ground-state configurations balance many energies and sometimes give surprising results.

items.title: Atomic radius goes UP across the lanthanides (then drops)
items.claim: Atomic radius generally decreases across a period: protons increase but the outer shell is the same. The 4f electrons in the lanthanides screen the nucleus so poorly that radius decreases throughout the row — and then the 5d and 6s elements after them are SMALLER than expected.
items.prompt: What's the consequence of this 'lanthanide contraction'?

options.text: Elements just after the lanthanides (Hf, Ta, W and below) have surprisingly small radii, almost identical to those of the elements above them in the same group (Zr, Nb, Mo) — so zirconium and hafnium have nearly identical chemistry and are very hard to separate
Atomic radius goes UP, not down, across the lanthanides

items.reveal:
Across the 14 lanthanides, atomic number rises by 14 but the added electrons go into 4f orbitals, which are 'inside' the 6s shell and screen the outer electrons very poorly. So the effective nuclear charge felt by the 6s shell grows steadily — the outer shell shrinks.

By the time you reach hafnium (Z=72, just after the lanthanides), the atomic radius is approximately the same as zirconium (Z=40) above it. Atomic radius is 159 pm for Zr, 156 pm for Hf — virtually identical.

The practical consequence: Zr and Hf are chemically almost indistinguishable and have to be separated by very fine techniques (typically ion-exchange chromatography). They are sold side by side. Hafnium controls in nuclear reactors depend on this.
items.why: Down-group similarity is taught; lateral similarity caused by f-shell shielding is a hidden consequence of the periodic table's full structure.
